facts.statement: The genus Bottosaurus was first described by Louis Agassiz in 1849.
Fossils of Bottosaurus date from the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous to the Paleocene epoch.
Bottosaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous and Early Paleocene in New Jersey, Texas, and possibly North Carolina and South Carolina.
facts.quote: Bottosaurus is an extinct genus of alligatorid from the Late Cretaceous-Early Paleocene of New Jersey, Texas, and possibly North Carolina and South Carolina.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic studies from the 2010s classify Bottosaurus within the subfamily Caimaninae, making it more closely related to modern caimans than to alligators.
facts.quote: 2010s phylogenetic studies have recovered Bottosaurus as a member of Alligatoridae within the subfamily Caimaninae, which indicates that Bottosaurus is more closely related to caimans than to alligators.

facts.statement: Bottosaurus possessed distinctively thick osteoderms that lacked the pitting found in most other crocodilians.
facts.quote: Bottosaurus had distinctively thick osteoderms that lacked the pitting of most other crocodylians.

facts.statement: The most common fossil remains of Bottosaurus are its unusual blunt, conical teeth adapted for crushing.
facts.quote: The unusual blunt, conical tribodont crushing teeth are the most common diagnostic material to fossilize and be recovered

facts.statement: Bottosaurus teeth featured a wrinkled enamel surface with prominent annual growth rings and vertical ridges.
facts.quote: The teeth had a "wrinkled" enamel surface and prominent annual rings with vertical ridges running down them.

facts.statement: The type species B. harlani had a short, massive lower jaw that was nearly circular in cross-section.
facts.quote: A short, massive lower jaw that is nearly circular in cross-section is evident from remains of the type species B. harlani.

facts.statement: A juvenile jaw of B. harlani found on the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary likely represents a mass death event (thanatoecoenosis) following the extinction event.
facts.quote: The fossil jaw of a juvenile B. harlani has been recorded from the Main Fossiliferous Layer of the Hornerstown Formation of New Jersey, which is located directly on the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary and likely represents a thanatoecoenosis in the aftermath of Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction event.

facts.statement: The species Bottosaurus fustidens was described from the middle Paleocene of western Texas.
facts.quote: Another species, Bottosaurus fustidens, has recently been described from the middle Paleocene (Tiffanian) of western Texas.

facts.statement: Bottosaurus is predominantly found in Late Cretaceous Maastrichtian strata, including the Hornerstown Formation, New Jersey Greensands, and Laramie Formation.
facts.quote: El género es hallado predominantemente en los estratos del Cretácico Superior de la etapa del Maastrichtiense, tales como los de la Formación Hornerstown, la Arenisca de Nueva Jersey y la Formación Laramie.

facts.statement: Additional fossils from South Carolina dating to the Danian and Thanetian stages show that Bottosaurus survived the Cretaceous-Tertiary extinction and lived through much of the early Paleogene before finally going extinct at the end of the Paleocene.
facts.quote: Material adicional se ha encontrado en la Formación Rhems y la Formación Williamsburg del Grupo Black Mingo de la planicie costera de Carolina del Sur que datan de las etapas del Daniense y el Tanetiano de la época del Paleoceno respectivamente, lo que muestra que Bottosaurus sobrevivió a la extinción masiva del Cretácico-Terciario y vivió durante buena parte del inicio del período Paleógeno en estas localidades antes de extinguirse finalmente al final del Paleoceno.

facts.statement: The time range for Bottosaurus is estimated from 83.6 to 56 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Thanetian (83.6 to 56 million years ago)

facts.statement: The Spanish Wikipedia entry classifies Bottosaurus within the family Crocodylidae.

rejected.statement: Fossil evidence from South Carolina suggests Bottosaurus survived the Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction event and lived through much of the early Paleogene.
rejected.quote: New material has been reported from the Rhems and Williamsburg Formations of the Black Mingo Group of the South Carolina coastal plain that dates back to the Danian and Thanetian stages of the Paleocene epoch, suggesting that Bottosaurus had survived the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event and lived through much of the early Paleogene period.
